The "winding up" of the sun (*takwīr al-shams*) is the corruption of its body, by the folding of its outer part into its inner part, such that its structure is disrupted, and with the disruption of its structure the order of its course is disrupted. From the expression *kawwara al-ʿimāma* ("he wound the turban"), meaning he inserted part of it into another part and wrapped it. Close to this usage is the usage of "folding" (*ṭayy*) in His saying: ﴿On the day We will fold up the heaven like the folding of a written scroll﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 104].

*Kuwwirat* has been interpreted with the meaning of *ghuwwirat* ("darkened"/"extinguished"). Al-Ṭabarī related this from Ibn Jubayr, and said: it is a word arabicized from Persian, and that its original form in Persian is *kūr bikr* (with a *ḍamma* on the first *kāf* and a sukūn on the final *rāʾ*). On this basis this word is counted among the arabicized words in the Qur'an. Ibn al-Subkī also counted it in his versified list of arabicized words in the Qur'an.

When the light of the sun disappears, the stars fall dispersing (*inkadarat*), because most of them shine from the reflection of the sun's light upon them.

*Inkidār* is the reflexive form (*muṭāwaʿ*) of *kaddarahu*, the doubled form, against the usual pattern; i.e., the stars have undergone *inkidār* from the "clouding" (*takdīr*) of the sun upon them when the reflection of its light left them. For this reason the reflexive form of *kaddara* is mentioned without mention of the agent of the clouding.

*Kudra* is the opposite of clarity, like the change in the colour of water and the like.

*Inkidār* has been interpreted as falling and swooping down, and they cited the verse of al-ʿAjjāj describing a falcon:

*He saw the ravens in the open space, and swooped down.*

Its meaning of falling is that some of them fall upon others and collide with them, because of the disruption of the system of gravitation that God established to hold them in place until a known term.

The "setting in motion" of the mountains (*tasyīr al-jibāl*) is their moving from their places through the shaking and quaking of the earth. This was discussed in Surat al-Naba'.

*ʿIshār* is the plural of *ʿushrāʾ*, which is the pregnant she-camel when she has reached ten months of pregnancy and is about to give birth; for camels carry for a full year. The *ʿishār* are the most valuable possessions of the Arabs. The meaning of *ʿuṭṭilat* is that they are left, not benefited from.

The statement is a metonymy (*kināya*) for people abandoning their work because of the intensity of the terror.

On this interpretation, this is among the signs of the Hour on earth, and so it fits with "and when the wild beasts are gathered."

It is also possible that the *ʿishār* are used as a metaphor (*istiʿāra*) for the clouds laden with rain, likened to the pregnant she-camel. This is not far from usage, for they apply such a metaphor to clouds, just as they applied the name *bikr* ("virgin/first-born") to a cloud in ʿAntara's words:

*Every free virgin [cloud] poured upon him, and they left every low ground like a dirham.*

So he applied to the abundantly watery cloud the name of the free virgin, i.e., the noble she-camel in her first pregnancy.

The meaning of the "suspension" of the clouds is that something befalls them that holds back their rain from falling, or it means that the heavy clouds do not gather and do not carry water; so the meaning of their suspension is their non-formation, and then drought follows on the earth, and people and livestock perish. On this interpretation, it is among the signs of the upper Hour, and so it fits with the folding of the sun and the dispersing of the stars.

[p. 143]

The *waḥsh* (wild beasts) is the plural of *waḥsh*, which is the wild animal that is not domesticated with people.

Their *ḥashr* (gathering) is their being gathered in one place, that is, one place on earth, when the end of the world approaches. The cause of their gathering may be a flood that engulfs the earth from the overflowing of the seas. Whenever it submerges a part of the earth, its beasts flee until they gather in one place seeking escape from destruction. This is suggested by the conjunction of "and when the seas are set boiling" with it.

This is mentioned with reference to the wild beasts as an indication of the intensity of the terror. The beasts, whose nature is to shun one another, gather in one place, and none of them attacks another out of extreme fear; they are distracted from their natural tendency toward aggression and predation. This is not the gathering by which people are gathered for reckoning; rather, this is a gathering in the world, and it is the one appropriate to the signs with which it is counted. Its meaning was related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

The *taskīr* of the seas (*taskīr al-biḥār*) is their overflowing. God said: ﴿and by the sea that is filled [with fire]﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 6] in Surat al-Ṭūr. What is meant is that their waters exceed the measure of their surfaces, and some of them mix with others; this is from the effects of the disruption of the strength of the air sphere that was pressing upon them. It occurs in the verse of Surat al-Infiṭār: ﴿and when the seas are burst forth﴾ [al-Infiṭār: 3]. When this happens, its water mixes with its sand, and so its colour changes.

It is said: *sajjara* (with doubling) and *sajara* (without doubling). Both have been read. The majority read it doubled (*sajjirat*), while Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb read it without doubling (*sujirat*).

His saying: ﴿and when the souls are paired﴾ begins the mention of the conditions occurring in the Hereafter on the Day of Resurrection. The shift to mentioning them is because they occur right after the six that preceded them, and it begins with the first of them, which is the pairing of the souls. *Tazwīj* is making one thing a mate (*zawj*) for another after both were singular. *Tazwīj* also means making things into similar types, as God said: ﴿and from all fruits He made in it two mates﴾ [al-Raʿd: 3]; for *zawj* is applied to a kind and a category of things. *Nufūs* is the plural of *nafs*, and *nafs* is applied to the spirit, as God said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾ [al-Fajr: 27] ﴿return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], and He said: ﴿Bring forth your souls﴾ [al-Anʿām: 93].

[p. 144]

*Nafs* is also applied to the person himself, as God said: ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Anʿām: 151], and He said: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumuʿa: 2], and He said: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another, [a greeting] from God﴾ [al-Nūr: 61], meaning: let the one entering greet those like him among the people.

So the meaning of *nufūs* here may be the spirits, i.e., the spirits are paired with the bodies assigned to them, so the spirit becomes a mate with the body after it had been singular, without a body, in the realm of spirits (*barzakh al-arwāḥ*). The bodies had been without spirits when they were recreated; i.e., when the spirits are given to the bodies. This is the resurrection, and it is the meaning that comes first to mind; it was related from ʿIkrima.

It is also possible that the meaning is: and when the persons are classified and sorted, and made into categories: believers, righteous, disbelievers, and wicked. God said: ﴿And you will be three kinds: the companions of the right, what are the companions of the right; and the companions of the left, what are the companions of the left; and the foremost﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 7] and so on.

Probably the purpose of this construction in conveying these two meanings is what the deviation from mentioning what the souls were paired with requires. The first stage of resurrection is the joining of spirits to their bodies, then the division of people into their ranks for gathering, as God said: ﴿Then it will be blown again, and behold they will be standing, looking﴾ [al-Zumar: 68], then He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], then He said: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be led to Paradise in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] and so on.

They have mentioned other meanings for the pairing of souls in this verse, which do not fit the context.

Because of the connection between the pairing of souls with bodies, the questioning of the buried infant girl is singled out for mention among what the criminals are asked about on the Day of Reckoning. That is because the return of spirits to bodies occurs after their separation through death, and death is either from an external bodily cause such as dissolution or sickness, or from aggressive transgression such as killing or fighting. Among the most heinous transgressions against taking spirits from their bodies is the transgression of fathers against the souls of their children through burying them alive, for God placed in human nature the eagerness of fathers to preserve their children, and made the two parents the cause of the existence of children. So burying alive is the most heinous of the deeds of the people of polytheism. The questioning of the buried infant girl is an allusive questioning, intended as a threat to her burier and to terrify him with punishment.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the questioning of the buried infant girl and the punishment of whoever buried her is the first matter to be judged on the Day of Resurrection,

[p. 145]

as the making of this questioning a time at which every soul knows what it has brought forth requires. So it is among the first things by which one knows at the time of recompense.

*Wa'd* is burying a girl child alive. It has been said that it is an inversion of *ādāhu*, meaning he burdened him, because it is the burdening of the buried one with dirt. Al-Zamakhsharī said in *al-Kashshāf*: A man, when a daughter was born to him and he wished to keep her alive, would dress her in a woollen or hair garment, to tend the camels and sheep in the desert. But if he wished to kill her, he would leave her until she was six years old, then say to her mother: "Perfume her and adorn her," until he took her to her in-laws, having dug a well for her in the desert. He would bring her to the well and say to her, "Look into it," then push her from behind and pour dirt over her until the well was level with the ground.

It was also said: a pregnant woman, when she was near her time, would dig a pit and give birth at its edge. If she gave birth to a girl she would throw her into the pit, and if she gave birth to a boy she would keep him. End of quote.

They used to do this out of fear of an enemy raid that would take their women captive, and out of fear of poverty in years of drought, because a male can seek earnings by raiding and other means, while a female is a dependent on her family. God said: ﴿And do not kill your children out of fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 31], and He said: ﴿And when one of them is given the news of [the birth of] a female, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses [rage]. He hides from the people because of the evil of what he has been informed of: Shall he keep it despite disgrace, or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they decide﴾ [al-Naḥl: 58].

Since the fear of disgrace at the birth of daughters has spread among them, its hatred has grown in their souls, and criminal impulses have stirred within them. A man hates to have a daughter born to him for this reason, and his wife hates to bear a daughter for fear of her husband leaving her. A man may also abandon his wife if she gives birth to a daughter.

Most nations have inherited this ignorance, though they differ in its degree. Among the sayings of some of them, when his daughter died: "What a fine in-law is the grave!"

Among the effects of this attitude is the deprivation of daughters from their fathers' wealth through various stratagems, such as endowing their property exclusively to males and not to females. Malik said: "That is from the custom of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam)," and he considered such a waqf (endowment) void. Many relatives of the deceased would pressure his daughters to renounce their right to their father's inheritance in favour of their brothers, in the heat of grief over their father's death. [Page 146] They would not refuse, and they regarded refusal as a shame upon them. If they did not comply, their relatives would sever ties with them.

In jurisprudence this matter is known as "the gifting of tribal daughters" (hibat banat al-qaba'il), and some scholars count it as a form of coercion.

Burying daughters alive (al-wa'd) was not practised by all tribes. It is said: the first of the tribes to bury daughters was Rabi'ah. Kindah used to bury daughters, and the Banu Tamim also did so. Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari of the Banu Tamim buried eight of his daughters before his conversion to Islam.

Burying daughters was not practised at all among Quraysh. Sa'sa'ah ibn Najiyah, the grandfather of al-Farazdaq, of the Banu Tamim, would ransom from his people whoever he knew intended to bury his daughter, with two pregnant she-camels and a male camel. It is said that he ransomed three hundred and sixty infants, and it is said seventy, and in al-Aghani it is said four hundred.

In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi: "Islam came when he had saved seventy girls from burial." A similar account appears in Ibn Qutaybah's Kitab al-Shu'ara'. There is a great gap between the two numbers, so perhaps one of them contains a distortion.

In directing the question to the buried infant, "For what sin was she killed?" in that gathering, there is the intimidation of her buriers, and the making of her question concern the identification of a sin that required her killing is a rebuke and censure of the one who buried her. The purpose is that her answer would be testimony against the one who buried her, so that his deserving of punishment would be greater and more evident.

The clause "for what sin was she killed" explains the clause "she was asked."

The word (ayy) is an interrogative noun, used to seek the distinguishing of one thing from among things that share a condition with it.

The interrogation in "for what sin" is rhetorical (taqriri), meaning it affirms a fact through a question. She was asked about identifying the sin that required her killing, rather than being asked about her killer, in order to increase the threat, because asking about the identification of the sin while the buryer who hears that question is certain that she has no sin signals to the buryer that he is not excused for what he did to her.

From the words of the Exalted, "She was asked: for what sin was she killed?" which occurs in a context of negating any sin in the buried infant that would necessitate her killing, one may derive an argument that the children of polytheists who die are not regarded as polytheists like their fathers. The first I have seen to address this argument is al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf [Page 147], who mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas used this meaning as proof. He said in al-Kashshaf: "In it is evidence that the children of polytheists are not punished, and since God has silenced the disbeliever through the innocence of the buried infant from sin, how ugly it would be for Him, who does not wrong even an atom's weight, to return to this silencing and do to her what would make her forget the punishment of the disgraced, the everlasting torment." It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about this and cited this verse as evidence. Thus he pointed to three proofs.

The first is the proof by implication (dalalat al-isharah), that is, because the words "for what sin was she killed?" indicate that she had no sin. This is a weak argument, because the sin whose existence is negated through an interrogation mixed with denial is only the sin that would license her father to bury her, not establishing the inviolability of her life and the sanctity of her blood, which is a separate question with its own details.

The second is the principle of attributing the doing of an ugly act to God, based on the Mu'tazilite principle of good and evil (al-tahsin wa al-taqbih), and their attribution of injustice to God if He punishes anyone without that person having done it. This is a disputed principle between the Ash'aris and the Mu'tazilites. For us, God's disposing of His servants is not described as unjust, contrary to their position. Moreover, this argument is built upon the foundation of the first argument, and you know that it is not free from refutation.

The third is what he attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, referring to what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted with his chain to 'Ikrimah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The children of polytheists are in Paradise; whoever claims they are in the Fire has denied the word of God: ﴿And when the buried infant is asked, for what sin was she killed?﴾." It has been answered regarding the report from Ibn 'Abbas that it does not reach the level of soundness, and this is a matter of the fundamentals of religion, in which only a decisive proof is sufficient.

Know that the sound hadiths concerning the ruling on the children of polytheists conflict. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the children or offspring of polytheists, and he said: "God knows best what they would have done." This answer may mean withholding judgement, that is, "God knows their state," like the word of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Book﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], in answer to Pharaoh's ﴿What then of the former generations?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51]. It may also be understood that the meaning is: God knows the state of each of them, had he grown up, what he would have done of disbelief or belief, that is, He would deal with him according to what He knows of his state.

[Page 148] Al-Bukhari and Muslim, with some variation in wording, related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition), then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian." The hadith continues. In Muslim's narration there is an addition: then Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite: ﴿The fitrah of God upon which He created mankind; there is no altering of God's creation; that is the upright religion﴾ [Al-Rum: 30]." This implies that they are born upon the fitrah of Islam until something from their parents or relatives or companions enters and changes them from it. This is the clearest indication used in this question.

Al-Mazari said in al-Mu'allim: "The scholars differed about them. The hadiths came with apparently differing meanings, and the divergence of these apparent meanings is the cause of the scholars' disagreement on this matter, and a definitive ruling here is far-fetched."

Abu Hurayrah's words, "Recite: ﴿the fitrah of God upon which He created mankind﴾" and so on, are a lamp that illuminates the way to reconcile these reports. A statement that is clearly on this point appears in the hadith of the dream, from Samurah ibn Jundub, where the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "As for the man in the garden, he is Ibrahim (peace be upon him); and as for the young children around him, every child who died upon the fitrah." Samurah said: some of the Muslims said: "O Messenger of God, and the children of polytheists?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "And the children of polytheists."

The scholars differed in their statements on the children of polytheists. Ibn al-Mubarak, Hammad ibn Salamah, Hammad ibn Zayd, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and al-Shafi'i said: they are in the will of God. The correct view on which the researchers and the majority agree is that they are in Paradise, and this is the apparent meaning of Abu Hurayrah's statement. The Azariqah held that the children of polytheists follow their fathers. Abu 'Ubayd said: "I asked Muhammad ibn al-Hasan about the hadith, 'Every child is born upon the fitrah,' and he said: that was at the beginning of Islam, before the obligatory duties were revealed and before jihad was made obligatory." Abu 'Ubayd said: "It seems he meant that if he were born upon the fitrah, they would not inherit from him, because he is a Muslim and they are disbelievers. When the obligations were prescribed contrary to that, it became permissible to call him a disbeliever, and it was known that he is born upon their religion."

There are many other opinions not attributed to any specific scholar and not resting on any sound report.

Al-Mazari mentioned that the children of the prophets are in Paradise by consensus, that the majority of scholars hold that the children of the rest of the believers are in Paradise, and that some scholars withheld judgement regarding them. Al-Nawawi said: "All scholars of the Muslims whose opinion counts have agreed that whoever of the children of Muslims dies is among the people of Paradise."

[Page 149] The majority read ﴿قُتِلَتْ﴾ (qutilat) with the first ta' lightened (tukhfif), while Abu Ja'far read it with it doubled (tashdid), which conveys the meaning that it was a severe, monstrous killing.

The literal meaning of "spreading the scrolls" (nashr al-suhuf) is opening the folds of the page, or releasing its rolling so that its writing may be read. It was mentioned in his words ﴿Rather, each man among them wishes to be given scrolls spread out﴾ [Al-Muddaththir: 52] in Surat al-Muddaththir, and at his words ﴿a Book which he will find spread open﴾ [Al-Isra': 13] in Surat al-Isra'.

What is meant is the scrolls of deeds. They are either literal scrolls different from the familiar scrolls, or figurative, applied to things in which the deeds of people are recorded. This has been mentioned more than once before.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿نُشِرَتْ﴾ (nushirat) with the shin lightened. The majority read it with the shin doubled, for intensity, because of the great number of scrolls spread.

Al-kashṭ (kashṭ) is the removal of the hide from a dead animal, and it is more general than salkh (skinning), because salkh is used only for removing the hide of cattle and sheep, not for removing the hide of camels; the latter is kashṭ and is not called salkh. The apparent meaning is that the removal occurs on the Day of Resurrection, because it is mentioned among the events of the Day of Resurrection, after His words ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ and ﴿And when the buried infant is asked﴾ and His words ﴿And when the scrolls are spread﴾.

It therefore appears that the sky will remain split and cleft, with the angels ascending between it and the place of assembly until the reckoning is completed. When the reckoning is finished, the sky will be removed from its place. So the sky is "stripped away," and what is stripped away is the realm of permanence. The word ﴿كُشِطَتْ﴾ (kushitat) is then a metaphor for removal.

It is also possible that this is among the events made signs of the Hour, and its mention was postponed for the sake of its connection with the mention of the spreading of the scrolls, because the angels, who are of the people of heaven, spread the scrolls. Thus this stripping is of the same kind as the splitting in His words ﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ [Al-Inshiqaq: 1] and the cleaving in His words ﴿When the sky is cleft﴾ [Al-Infitar: 1] up to His words ﴿every soul will know what it has sent forward and left behind﴾ [Al-Infitar: 5]. The stripping is then of some parts of the sky, and what is stripped from is some other part. It is of the same kind as His words: ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of a needle﴾ [Al-A'raf: 40], and of the same kind as the folding in His words: ﴿The Day We fold up the heaven like the folding of a scroll for writings; as We originated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 104], since its apparent meaning is that the folding of the sky is connected with the re-creation. Thus the signs occurring before resurrection become seven, and the events occurring after resurrection become five.

Al-jahim (al-jahim), in origin, is a fire of many layers of fuel, of wood and the like, some above others. It became a proper name by predominance for Jahannam, the abode of punishment in the Hereafter, in the terminology of the Qur'an. Its tasting (taS'ir) or ignition (is'ar) means its kindling, that is, it was prepared for the punishment of those upon whom punishment is due.

Nafi', Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read (suc'[c]irat) with the 'ayn doubled, for intensification of the kindling. The rest read it with the lightened form.

Paradise is contrasted with the Fire, the abode of bliss. The name "Jannah" is a proper name by predominance for the abode of bliss. ﴿وَأُزْلِفَتْ﴾ (wa-uzlifat) means it was brought near, and zulfa means nearness. That is, Paradise was brought near to its people, that is, it was made close to their place of assembly, such that there is no hardship for them in reaching it, and that is an honour for them.

Know that the fronting of the predicate-subject (musnad ilayh) in the twelve clauses opened with the word (idha) from His saying, ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾, up to here, and the predicating of it with a verbal predicate, although it could have been said: "When the sun is wrapped up, and when the stars fall," and so on, as in His saying, ﴿Then when the sky splits open and becomes red like rose, like oil﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], is for the purpose of conveying concern with those reports which are made into signs of the Day of Resurrection, as a means of drawing attention to its signs and thereby to the Day itself and to affirming its occurrence.

The lengthy mention of those clauses creates suspense for the answer that comes after them, His saying, ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾.

The clause ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ is governed by the repeated words "idha" (when) in terms of its dependence on it.

It is reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he recited the beginning of this surah, and when he reached ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾, he said: "For this the narrative was set in motion." That is, it is the answer of the oath. The meaning of "will know" is that it will be known by what it has presented, so it will know it.

His saying, "a soul" (nafs), is an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional, intended to be general; that is, every soul will know what it has presented. Deriving generality from an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is achieved by a contextual indicator showing that no specific individual of the kind is intended. The indicator here is that the word "nafs" occurs in the answer to these conditions, of which it does not occur to the mind that they could be conditions for a single person. And Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it did of good present, and what it did of evil﴾ [Al 'Imran: 30].

Ihdar (presenting) means making a thing present.

The meaning of ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ is the attainment of certainty about what it had no knowledge of, from the realities of its deeds, whose knowledge of them had been scattered: some of it known in a way other than its true form, some of it known in its outward form while its consequences were unknown, and some of it forgotten. Thus the knowledge that people had in the worldly life was treated as if it were non-existence of knowledge, and knowledge of their deeds, good or bad, is affirmed for them on that Day, so that they know what they had no knowledge of, of what they had belittled of their deeds, and remember what they had known before. The remembering of what was forgotten and neglected is a kind of knowledge.

What it has presented is what it sent ahead of deeds. Since the effects of deeds become manifest on that Day, in reward and punishment, the manifestation of their effects is expressed by "presenting," because of its resemblance to it, just as provision is presented to the traveler. Thus in the verb "presented" (ahdarat) there is a metaphor. The term is also applied to that preparation, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the one who asked him, "When is the Hour?": "What have you prepared for it?"

The presenting is attributed to souls because they are the doers of the deeds whose recompense becomes manifest on that Day. This attribution is the attribution of an act to the cause of its doing. Thus two figurative usages occur here: a linguistic metaphor and a rational metaphor. Their literal form is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it did of good present, and what it did of evil﴾ [Al 'Imran: 30].

The soul's knowledge of the recompense of its deeds is made to occur upon the gathering of all the conditions mentioned in the twelve clauses; because some of the states contained in the conditions coincide with the soul's knowledge of its deeds, namely the six states mentioned last, and some of the states had occurred shortly before, namely the six states mentioned first. So the near is treated as the coinciding, and therefore all of them are made conditions for "idha."

[p. 141]

**Surah 81, verses 1–14 (Part 1 of 3)**

﴿When the sun is wound up,﴾ ﴿and when the stars fall, dispersing,﴾ ﴿and when the mountains are set moving,﴾ ﴿and when the pregnant camels are abandoned,﴾ ﴿and when the wild beasts are gathered,﴾ ﴿and when the seas are set boiling,﴾ ﴿and when the souls are paired,﴾ ﴿and when the buried infant girl is asked﴾ ﴿for what sin she was killed,﴾ ﴿and when the scrolls are spread open,﴾ ﴿and when the sky is stripped away,﴾ ﴿and when Hellfire is kindled,﴾ ﴿and when Paradise is brought near,﴾ ﴿each soul will know what it has brought forth.﴾

The opening with *idhā* (when) is an arresting opening, because *idhā* is a temporal adverb that calls for a complement, and it is also a conditional that signals the mention of an answer after it. When the listener hears it, he awaits what will come after it, and so when he hears it his soul becomes fully absorbed, especially with the amplification (*iṭnāb*, elaboration by repetition) through the repetition of the word *idhā*.

[The repetition of] the number of clauses to which it is attached, twelve times, is also a case of *iṭnāb*: the repetition of the word *idhā* after the conjunction *wāw* in these coordinated clauses is *iṭnāb*, and this *iṭnāb* is required by the intention of awe-inspiring magnification (*tahwīl*), and magnification is one of the requirements of *iṭnāb* and repetition, as in the poem of al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbbād al-Bakrī:

*Bring close to me the tethering-place of the ostrich,*
*etc.*

In the repetition of *idhā* there is an indication that the content of each of these twelve clauses is independently established upon the occurrence of the content of the answer-clause, regardless of the difference in the time at which the conditions occur. For the time of the questioning of the buried infant girl and the spreading of the scrolls is closer to the souls' knowledge of what they have brought forth than the time of the coiling of the sun and what is coordinated with it, of what occurs before resurrection.

[p. 142 — hmm, the page marker is 141 in source before this; the next marker "صفحة ١٤١" appeared here.]

Twelve events are mentioned in these verses: six of them occur at the end of the worldly life, and six of them occur in the Hereafter.

The clauses that were made conditions of *idhā* in this verse begin with the subject (*al-musnad ilayhi*) followed by a verbal predicate, rather than being verbal clauses, and without assuming omitted verbs that the mentioned verbs would explain. This supports the view of the grammarians of Kufa that the condition of *idhā* may be a non-verbal clause, which is the preferred view, because *idhā* is not well established as a conditional particle. This construction is for the purpose of emphasizing what the verbs are predicated of, which are usually conditions of *idhā*; beginning with them is more effective in awe-inspiring magnification and arousing interest, and in order that the fronting of the subject before the verbal predicate convey the strengthening and affirmation of the judgment in all those clauses, in refutation of those who deny it. For this reason it says *idhā al-shamsu kuwwirat* ("when the sun is wound up") and not *idhā kuwwirat al-shamsu*, and the same applies to its counterparts.

The answer to the twelve conditions is His saying: ﴿each soul will know what it has brought forth﴾, and the temporal phrases that carry the meaning of a condition are attached to it.

The form of the past tense in the twelve clauses that come as conditions of *idhā* is used with the meaning of the future, to alert to the certainty of the occurrence of the condition.

The "winding up" of the sun (*takwīr al-shams*) is the corruption of its body, by the folding of its outer part into its inner part, such that its structure is disrupted, and with the disruption of its structure the order of its course is disrupted. From the expression *kawwara al-ʿimāma* ("he wound the turban"), meaning he inserted part of it into another part and wrapped it. Close to this usage is the usage of "folding" (*ṭayy*) in His saying: ﴿On the day We will fold up the heaven like the folding of a written scroll﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 104].

*Kuwwirat* has been interpreted with the meaning of *ghuwwirat* ("darkened"/"extinguished"). Al-Ṭabarī related this from Ibn Jubayr, and said: it is a word arabicized from Persian, and that its original form in Persian is *kūr bikr* (with a *ḍamma* on the first *kāf* and a sukūn on the final *rāʾ*). On this basis this word is counted among the arabicized words in the Qur'an. Ibn al-Subkī also counted it in his versified list of arabicized words in the Qur'an.

When the light of the sun disappears, the stars fall dispersing (*inkadarat*), because most of them shine from the reflection of the sun's light upon them.

*Inkidār* is the reflexive form (*muṭāwaʿ*) of *kaddarahu*, the doubled form, against the usual pattern; i.e., the stars have undergone *inkidār* from the "clouding" (*takdīr*) of the sun upon them when the reflection of its light left them. For this reason the reflexive form of *kaddara* is mentioned without mention of the agent of the clouding.

*Kudra* is the opposite of clarity, like the change in the colour of water and the like.

*Inkidār* has been interpreted as falling and swooping down, and they cited the verse of al-ʿAjjāj describing a falcon:

*He saw the ravens in the open space, and swooped down.*

Its meaning of falling is that some of them fall upon others and collide with them, because of the disruption of the system of gravitation that God established to hold them in place until a known term.

The "setting in motion" of the mountains (*tasyīr al-jibāl*) is their moving from their places through the shaking and quaking of the earth. This was discussed in Surat al-Naba'.

*ʿIshār* is the plural of *ʿushrāʾ*, which is the pregnant she-camel when she has reached ten months of pregnancy and is about to give birth; for camels carry for a full year. The *ʿishār* are the most valuable possessions of the Arabs. The meaning of *ʿuṭṭilat* is that they are left, not benefited from.

The statement is a metonymy (*kināya*) for people abandoning their work because of the intensity of the terror.

On this interpretation, this is among the signs of the Hour on earth, and so it fits with "and when the wild beasts are gathered."

It is also possible that the *ʿishār* are used as a metaphor (*istiʿāra*) for the clouds laden with rain, likened to the pregnant she-camel. This is not far from usage, for they apply such a metaphor to clouds, just as they applied the name *bikr* ("virgin/first-born") to a cloud in ʿAntara's words:

*Every free virgin [cloud] poured upon him, and they left every low ground like a dirham.*

So he applied to the abundantly watery cloud the name of the free virgin, i.e., the noble she-camel in her first pregnancy.

The meaning of the "suspension" of the clouds is that something befalls them that holds back their rain from falling, or it means that the heavy clouds do not gather and do not carry water; so the meaning of their suspension is their non-formation, and then drought follows on the earth, and people and livestock perish. On this interpretation, it is among the signs of the upper Hour, and so it fits with the folding of the sun and the dispersing of the stars.

[p. 143]

The *waḥsh* (wild beasts) is the plural of *waḥsh*, which is the wild animal that is not domesticated with people.

Their *ḥashr* (gathering) is their being gathered in one place, that is, one place on earth, when the end of the world approaches. The cause of their gathering may be a flood that engulfs the earth from the overflowing of the seas. Whenever it submerges a part of the earth, its beasts flee until they gather in one place seeking escape from destruction. This is suggested by the conjunction of "and when the seas are set boiling" with it.

This is mentioned with reference to the wild beasts as an indication of the intensity of the terror. The beasts, whose nature is to shun one another, gather in one place, and none of them attacks another out of extreme fear; they are distracted from their natural tendency toward aggression and predation. This is not the gathering by which people are gathered for reckoning; rather, this is a gathering in the world, and it is the one appropriate to the signs with which it is counted. Its meaning was related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

The *taskīr* of the seas (*taskīr al-biḥār*) is their overflowing. God said: ﴿and by the sea that is filled [with fire]﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 6] in Surat al-Ṭūr. What is meant is that their waters exceed the measure of their surfaces, and some of them mix with others; this is from the effects of the disruption of the strength of the air sphere that was pressing upon them. It occurs in the verse of Surat al-Infiṭār: ﴿and when the seas are burst forth﴾ [al-Infiṭār: 3]. When this happens, its water mixes with its sand, and so its colour changes.

It is said: *sajjara* (with doubling) and *sajara* (without doubling). Both have been read. The majority read it doubled (*sajjirat*), while Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb read it without doubling (*sujirat*).

His saying: ﴿and when the souls are paired﴾ begins the mention of the conditions occurring in the Hereafter on the Day of Resurrection. The shift to mentioning them is because they occur right after the six that preceded them, and it begins with the first of them, which is the pairing of the souls. *Tazwīj* is making one thing a mate (*zawj*) for another after both were singular. *Tazwīj* also means making things into similar types, as God said: ﴿and from all fruits He made in it two mates﴾ [al-Raʿd: 3]; for *zawj* is applied to a kind and a category of things. *Nufūs* is the plural of *nafs*, and *nafs* is applied to the spirit, as God said: ﴿O soul at peace﴾ [al-Fajr: 27] ﴿return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], and He said: ﴿Bring forth your souls﴾ [al-Anʿām: 93].

[p. 144]

*Nafs* is also applied to the person himself, as God said: ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Anʿām: 151], and He said: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumuʿa: 2], and He said: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another, [a greeting] from God﴾ [al-Nūr: 61], meaning: let the one entering greet those like him among the people.

So the meaning of *nufūs* here may be the spirits, i.e., the spirits are paired with the bodies assigned to them, so the spirit becomes a mate with the body after it had been singular, without a body, in the realm of spirits (*barzakh al-arwāḥ*). The bodies had been without spirits when they were recreated; i.e., when the spirits are given to the bodies. This is the resurrection, and it is the meaning that comes first to mind; it was related from ʿIkrima.

It is also possible that the meaning is: and when the persons are classified and sorted, and made into categories: believers, righteous, disbelievers, and wicked. God said: ﴿And you will be three kinds: the companions of the right, what are the companions of the right; and the companions of the left, what are the companions of the left; and the foremost﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 7] and so on.

Probably the purpose of this construction in conveying these two meanings is what the deviation from mentioning what the souls were paired with requires. The first stage of resurrection is the joining of spirits to their bodies, then the division of people into their ranks for gathering, as God said: ﴿Then it will be blown again, and behold they will be standing, looking﴾ [al-Zumar: 68], then He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], then He said: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be led to Paradise in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] and so on.

They have mentioned other meanings for the pairing of souls in this verse, which do not fit the context.

Because of the connection between the pairing of souls with bodies, the questioning of the buried infant girl is singled out for mention among what the criminals are asked about on the Day of Reckoning. That is because the return of spirits to bodies occurs after their separation through death, and death is either from an external bodily cause such as dissolution or sickness, or from aggressive transgression such as killing or fighting. Among the most heinous transgressions against taking spirits from their bodies is the transgression of fathers against the souls of their children through burying them alive, for God placed in human nature the eagerness of fathers to preserve their children, and made the two parents the cause of the existence of children. So burying alive is the most heinous of the deeds of the people of polytheism. The questioning of the buried infant girl is an allusive questioning, intended as a threat to her burier and to terrify him with punishment.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the questioning of the buried infant girl and the punishment of whoever buried her is the first matter to be judged on the Day of Resurrection,

[p. 145]

as the making of this questioning a time at which every soul knows what it has brought forth requires. So it is among the first things by which one knows at the time of recompense.

*Wa'd* is burying a girl child alive. It has been said that it is an inversion of *ādāhu*, meaning he burdened him, because it is the burdening of the buried one with dirt. Al-Zamakhsharī said in *al-Kashshāf*: A man, when a daughter was born to him and he wished to keep her alive, would dress her in a woollen or hair garment, to tend the camels and sheep in the desert. But if he wished to kill her, he would leave her until she was six years old, then say to her mother: "Perfume her and adorn her," until he took her to her in-laws, having dug a well for her in the desert. He would bring her to the well and say to her, "Look into it," then push her from behind and pour dirt over her until the well was level with the ground.

It was also said: a pregnant woman, when she was near her time, would dig a pit and give birth at its edge. If she gave birth to a girl she would throw her into the pit, and if she gave birth to a boy she would keep him. End of quote.

They used to do this out of fear of an enemy raid that would take their women captive, and out of fear of poverty in years of drought, because a male can seek earnings by raiding and other means, while a female is a dependent on her family. God said: ﴿And do not kill your children out of fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 31], and He said: ﴿And when one of them is given the news of [the birth of] a female, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses [rage]. He hides from the people because of the evil of what he has been informed of: Shall he keep it despite disgrace, or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they decide﴾ [al-Naḥl: 58].

Since the fear of disgrace at the birth of daughters has spread among them, its hatred has grown in their souls, and criminal impulses have stirred within them. A man hates to have a daughter born to him for this reason, and his wife hates to bear a daughter for fear of her husband leaving her. A man may also abandon his wife if she gives birth to a daughter.

Most nations have inherited this ignorance, though they differ in its degree. Among the sayings of some of them, when his daughter died: "What a fine in-law is the grave!"

Among the effects of this attitude is the deprivation of daughters from their fathers' wealth through various stratagems, such as endowing their property exclusively to males and not to females. Malik said: "That is from the custom of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam)," and he considered such a waqf (endowment) void. Many relatives of the deceased would pressure his daughters to renounce their right to their father's inheritance in favour of their brothers, in the heat of grief over their father's death. [Page 146] They would not refuse, and they regarded refusal as a shame upon them. If they did not comply, their relatives would sever ties with them.

In jurisprudence this matter is known as "the gifting of tribal daughters" (hibat banat al-qaba'il), and some scholars count it as a form of coercion.

Burying daughters alive (al-wa'd) was not practised by all tribes. It is said: the first of the tribes to bury daughters was Rabi'ah. Kindah used to bury daughters, and the Banu Tamim also did so. Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari of the Banu Tamim buried eight of his daughters before his conversion to Islam.

Burying daughters was not practised at all among Quraysh. Sa'sa'ah ibn Najiyah, the grandfather of al-Farazdaq, of the Banu Tamim, would ransom from his people whoever he knew intended to bury his daughter, with two pregnant she-camels and a male camel. It is said that he ransomed three hundred and sixty infants, and it is said seventy, and in al-Aghani it is said four hundred.

In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi: "Islam came when he had saved seventy girls from burial." A similar account appears in Ibn Qutaybah's Kitab al-Shu'ara'. There is a great gap between the two numbers, so perhaps one of them contains a distortion.

In directing the question to the buried infant, "For what sin was she killed?" in that gathering, there is the intimidation of her buriers, and the making of her question concern the identification of a sin that required her killing is a rebuke and censure of the one who buried her. The purpose is that her answer would be testimony against the one who buried her, so that his deserving of punishment would be greater and more evident.

The clause "for what sin was she killed" explains the clause "she was asked."

The word (ayy) is an interrogative noun, used to seek the distinguishing of one thing from among things that share a condition with it.

The interrogation in "for what sin" is rhetorical (taqriri), meaning it affirms a fact through a question. She was asked about identifying the sin that required her killing, rather than being asked about her killer, in order to increase the threat, because asking about the identification of the sin while the buryer who hears that question is certain that she has no sin signals to the buryer that he is not excused for what he did to her.

From the words of the Exalted, "She was asked: for what sin was she killed?" which occurs in a context of negating any sin in the buried infant that would necessitate her killing, one may derive an argument that the children of polytheists who die are not regarded as polytheists like their fathers. The first I have seen to address this argument is al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf [Page 147], who mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas used this meaning as proof. He said in al-Kashshaf: "In it is evidence that the children of polytheists are not punished, and since God has silenced the disbeliever through the innocence of the buried infant from sin, how ugly it would be for Him, who does not wrong even an atom's weight, to return to this silencing and do to her what would make her forget the punishment of the disgraced, the everlasting torment." It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about this and cited this verse as evidence. Thus he pointed to three proofs.

The first is the proof by implication (dalalat al-isharah), that is, because the words "for what sin was she killed?" indicate that she had no sin. This is a weak argument, because the sin whose existence is negated through an interrogation mixed with denial is only the sin that would license her father to bury her, not establishing the inviolability of her life and the sanctity of her blood, which is a separate question with its own details.

The second is the principle of attributing the doing of an ugly act to God, based on the Mu'tazilite principle of good and evil (al-tahsin wa al-taqbih), and their attribution of injustice to God if He punishes anyone without that person having done it. This is a disputed principle between the Ash'aris and the Mu'tazilites. For us, God's disposing of His servants is not described as unjust, contrary to their position. Moreover, this argument is built upon the foundation of the first argument, and you know that it is not free from refutation.

The third is what he attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, referring to what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted with his chain to 'Ikrimah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The children of polytheists are in Paradise; whoever claims they are in the Fire has denied the word of God: ﴿And when the buried infant is asked, for what sin was she killed?﴾." It has been answered regarding the report from Ibn 'Abbas that it does not reach the level of soundness, and this is a matter of the fundamentals of religion, in which only a decisive proof is sufficient.

Know that the sound hadiths concerning the ruling on the children of polytheists conflict. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the children or offspring of polytheists, and he said: "God knows best what they would have done." This answer may mean withholding judgement, that is, "God knows their state," like the word of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Book﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], in answer to Pharaoh's ﴿What then of the former generations?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51]. It may also be understood that the meaning is: God knows the state of each of them, had he grown up, what he would have done of disbelief or belief, that is, He would deal with him according to what He knows of his state.

[Page 148] Al-Bukhari and Muslim, with some variation in wording, related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition), then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian." The hadith continues. In Muslim's narration there is an addition: then Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite: ﴿The fitrah of God upon which He created mankind; there is no altering of God's creation; that is the upright religion﴾ [Al-Rum: 30]." This implies that they are born upon the fitrah of Islam until something from their parents or relatives or companions enters and changes them from it. This is the clearest indication used in this question.

Al-Mazari said in al-Mu'allim: "The scholars differed about them. The hadiths came with apparently differing meanings, and the divergence of these apparent meanings is the cause of the scholars' disagreement on this matter, and a definitive ruling here is far-fetched."

Abu Hurayrah's words, "Recite: ﴿the fitrah of God upon which He created mankind﴾" and so on, are a lamp that illuminates the way to reconcile these reports. A statement that is clearly on this point appears in the hadith of the dream, from Samurah ibn Jundub, where the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "As for the man in the garden, he is Ibrahim (peace be upon him); and as for the young children around him, every child who died upon the fitrah." Samurah said: some of the Muslims said: "O Messenger of God, and the children of polytheists?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "And the children of polytheists."

The scholars differed in their statements on the children of polytheists. Ibn al-Mubarak, Hammad ibn Salamah, Hammad ibn Zayd, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and al-Shafi'i said: they are in the will of God. The correct view on which the researchers and the majority agree is that they are in Paradise, and this is the apparent meaning of Abu Hurayrah's statement. The Azariqah held that the children of polytheists follow their fathers. Abu 'Ubayd said: "I asked Muhammad ibn al-Hasan about the hadith, 'Every child is born upon the fitrah,' and he said: that was at the beginning of Islam, before the obligatory duties were revealed and before jihad was made obligatory." Abu 'Ubayd said: "It seems he meant that if he were born upon the fitrah, they would not inherit from him, because he is a Muslim and they are disbelievers. When the obligations were prescribed contrary to that, it became permissible to call him a disbeliever, and it was known that he is born upon their religion."

There are many other opinions not attributed to any specific scholar and not resting on any sound report.

Al-Mazari mentioned that the children of the prophets are in Paradise by consensus, that the majority of scholars hold that the children of the rest of the believers are in Paradise, and that some scholars withheld judgement regarding them. Al-Nawawi said: "All scholars of the Muslims whose opinion counts have agreed that whoever of the children of Muslims dies is among the people of Paradise."

[Page 149] The majority read ﴿قُتِلَتْ﴾ (qutilat) with the first ta' lightened (tukhfif), while Abu Ja'far read it with it doubled (tashdid), which conveys the meaning that it was a severe, monstrous killing.

The literal meaning of "spreading the scrolls" (nashr al-suhuf) is opening the folds of the page, or releasing its rolling so that its writing may be read. It was mentioned in his words ﴿Rather, each man among them wishes to be given scrolls spread out﴾ [Al-Muddaththir: 52] in Surat al-Muddaththir, and at his words ﴿a Book which he will find spread open﴾ [Al-Isra': 13] in Surat al-Isra'.

What is meant is the scrolls of deeds. They are either literal scrolls different from the familiar scrolls, or figurative, applied to things in which the deeds of people are recorded. This has been mentioned more than once before.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿نُشِرَتْ﴾ (nushirat) with the shin lightened. The majority read it with the shin doubled, for intensity, because of the great number of scrolls spread.

Al-kashṭ (kashṭ) is the removal of the hide from a dead animal, and it is more general than salkh (skinning), because salkh is used only for removing the hide of cattle and sheep, not for removing the hide of camels; the latter is kashṭ and is not called salkh. The apparent meaning is that the removal occurs on the Day of Resurrection, because it is mentioned among the events of the Day of Resurrection, after His words ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ and ﴿And when the buried infant is asked﴾ and His words ﴿And when the scrolls are spread﴾.

It therefore appears that the sky will remain split and cleft, with the angels ascending between it and the place of assembly until the reckoning is completed. When the reckoning is finished, the sky will be removed from its place. So the sky is "stripped away," and what is stripped away is the realm of permanence. The word ﴿كُشِطَتْ﴾ (kushitat) is then a metaphor for removal.

It is also possible that this is among the events made signs of the Hour, and its mention was postponed for the sake of its connection with the mention of the spreading of the scrolls, because the angels, who are of the people of heaven, spread the scrolls. Thus this stripping is of the same kind as the splitting in His words ﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ [Al-Inshiqaq: 1] and the cleaving in His words ﴿When the sky is cleft﴾ [Al-Infitar: 1] up to His words ﴿every soul will know what it has sent forward and left behind﴾ [Al-Infitar: 5]. The stripping is then of some parts of the sky, and what is stripped from is some other part. It is of the same kind as His words: ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of a needle﴾ [Al-A'raf: 40], and of the same kind as the folding in His words: ﴿The Day We fold up the heaven like the folding of a scroll for writings; as We originated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 104], since its apparent meaning is that the folding of the sky is connected with the re-creation. Thus the signs occurring before resurrection become seven, and the events occurring after resurrection become five.

Al-jahim (al-jahim), in origin, is a fire of many layers of fuel, of wood and the like, some above others. It became a proper name by predominance for Jahannam, the abode of punishment in the Hereafter, in the terminology of the Qur'an. Its tasting (taS'ir) or ignition (is'ar) means its kindling, that is, it was prepared for the punishment of those upon whom punishment is due.

Nafi', Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read (suc'[c]irat) with the 'ayn doubled, for intensification of the kindling. The rest read it with the lightened form.

Paradise is contrasted with the Fire, the abode of bliss. The name "Jannah" is a proper name by predominance for the abode of bliss. ﴿وَأُزْلِفَتْ﴾ (wa-uzlifat) means it was brought near, and zulfa means nearness. That is, Paradise was brought near to its people, that is, it was made close to their place of assembly, such that there is no hardship for them in reaching it, and that is an honour for them.

Know that the fronting of the predicate-subject (musnad ilayh) in the twelve clauses opened with the word (idha) from His saying, ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾, up to here, and the predicating of it with a verbal predicate, although it could have been said: "When the sun is wrapped up, and when the stars fall," and so on, as in His saying, ﴿Then when the sky splits open and becomes red like rose, like oil﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], is for the purpose of conveying concern with those reports which are made into signs of the Day of Resurrection, as a means of drawing attention to its signs and thereby to the Day itself and to affirming its occurrence.

The lengthy mention of those clauses creates suspense for the answer that comes after them, His saying, ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾.

The clause ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ is governed by the repeated words "idha" (when) in terms of its dependence on it.

It is reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he recited the beginning of this surah, and when he reached ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾, he said: "For this the narrative was set in motion." That is, it is the answer of the oath. The meaning of "will know" is that it will be known by what it has presented, so it will know it.

His saying, "a soul" (nafs), is an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional, intended to be general; that is, every soul will know what it has presented. Deriving generality from an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is achieved by a contextual indicator showing that no specific individual of the kind is intended. The indicator here is that the word "nafs" occurs in the answer to these conditions, of which it does not occur to the mind that they could be conditions for a single person. And Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it did of good present, and what it did of evil﴾ [Al 'Imran: 30].

Ihdar (presenting) means making a thing present.

The meaning of ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ is the attainment of certainty about what it had no knowledge of, from the realities of its deeds, whose knowledge of them had been scattered: some of it known in a way other than its true form, some of it known in its outward form while its consequences were unknown, and some of it forgotten. Thus the knowledge that people had in the worldly life was treated as if it were non-existence of knowledge, and knowledge of their deeds, good or bad, is affirmed for them on that Day, so that they know what they had no knowledge of, of what they had belittled of their deeds, and remember what they had known before. The remembering of what was forgotten and neglected is a kind of knowledge.

What it has presented is what it sent ahead of deeds. Since the effects of deeds become manifest on that Day, in reward and punishment, the manifestation of their effects is expressed by "presenting," because of its resemblance to it, just as provision is presented to the traveler. Thus in the verb "presented" (ahdarat) there is a metaphor. The term is also applied to that preparation, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the one who asked him, "When is the Hour?": "What have you prepared for it?"

The presenting is attributed to souls because they are the doers of the deeds whose recompense becomes manifest on that Day. This attribution is the attribution of an act to the cause of its doing. Thus two figurative usages occur here: a linguistic metaphor and a rational metaphor. Their literal form is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it did of good present, and what it did of evil﴾ [Al 'Imran: 30].

The soul's knowledge of the recompense of its deeds is made to occur upon the gathering of all the conditions mentioned in the twelve clauses; because some of the states contained in the conditions coincide with the soul's knowledge of its deeds, namely the six states mentioned last, and some of the states had occurred shortly before, namely the six states mentioned first. So the near is treated as the coinciding, and therefore all of them are made conditions for "idha."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 81, verses 15–21:

Page 152
﴿So I swear by the receding stars,﴾ ﴿the ones that run and hide,﴾ ﴿and by the night when it departs,﴾ ﴿and by the dawn when it breathes,﴾ ﴿that this is indeed the word of a noble messenger,﴾ ﴿endowed with power, held in high esteem by the Lord of the Throne,﴾ ﴿obeyed there, and trustworthy.﴾

The fa' (فاء) here marks the consequence of the oath, and its answer is linked to the preceding discourse, indicating what came before. It serves as a preface to what follows the fa'. The preceding discourse established the reality of the Resurrection and the requital, which they had denied, and had rejected the Qur'an that warned them of it. When the warning concerning it was fulfilled and its signs were mentioned, there followed from it the affirmation of the Qur'an that warned them, and that it is revealed from Allah.

Thus the sequencing here is both a sequencing of meaning and a sequencing of mention together. The oath has also come as a mere sequencing of one statement upon another, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

"So I swore by the House around which men circled, sons of Quraysh and Jurhum,"

following the nasib (amatory prelude) of his Mu'allaqa, which the content after the oath does not follow from. He intended by it only that what preceded was for the sake of turning to what follows the fa'. By this the superiority of the sequencing in this verse over the sequencing of Zuhayr's line becomes apparent. The meaning of "lā uqsimu" is the making of an oath, and "lā" has been considered superfluous; this was discussed at His words, ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75] in Surat al-Waqi'ah.

The oath is intended to emphasize and confirm the report, and the attributes of the things sworn by have been incorporated into it to indicate the perfection of Allah's power.

Al-khunnas (الخُنَّس) is the plural of khanisah, which is the one that hides, i.e., conceals itself. It is said: the cow and the gazelle "khanisat" when they hid in their kinās (كناس, resting place).

Al-jawari (الجَوارِي) is the plural of jariyah, which is the one that runs, i.e., moves swiftly.

Al-kunnas (الكُنَّس) is the plural of kanisah. It is said: the gazelle "kanasa" when it entered its kinās (with a kasrah on the kaf), which is the den it takes for lodging.

These attributes are intended as figurative attributes, because the majority hold that what is meant by the things they describe is the stars. They are described thus because they are hidden from view during the day, so they are likened to wild animals concealed in trees or the like. Hence it is said "al-khunnas," and this is from the excellent figures of speech: khunus is the concealment of wild animals from the sight of hunters and the like, without settling in a den. Likewise the stars, since they are not seen during the day due to the predominance of the sun's rays over their horizon, yet they are still present in their risings.

Thus the rising of a star is likened to the emergence of a wild animal from its den, and the movement of its appearance to the observer is likened to the running of the wild animal as it comes out of its den in the morning. Labid said:

"Until the darkness withdrew and it shone forth, its arrows (rays) slipped from the dust in the early morning."

Its setting after its course is likened to the wild animals entering their dens, which is an excellent figure of speech. So His words "bi-l-khunnas" constitute a metaphor, and "al-jawari al-kunnas" are two elements that complete (tarshih) the metaphor.

From the totality of the three attributes there arises something resembling a riddle, whereby one may suppose the things described are gazelles or wild beasts, since those attributes are in reality properties of wild beasts. Riddles are a pleasing method among the eloquent Arabs, and they are rare in their speech. One of their poets, whose verse is among the evidences of Arabic grammar, said:

"I said: lend me the adze, perhaps I may dig with it a grave for a white, noble man."

He meant that he would make with it a sheath for a polished, Indian sword.

It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Ibn 'Abbas that these attributes are to be taken in their well-known literal senses, and that Allah swore by gazelles and wild cattle.

Page 153

The known practice in the oaths of the Qur'an is that they are by great things that indicate the power of Allah, or by blessed things.

Then the oath by the night was joined to the oath by the stars, due to the correspondence of the stars' movement in the night, and because the alternation of night and day is among the greatest manifestations of divine wisdom in this world.

Ibn 'Ashur on Surah 81 (continued)

'Asa'sa al-layl ('as'asa al-layl) means the night was 'as'as, with 'as'asan and 'as'asah. Mujahid, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, said: it advanced with its darkness. Mujahid also said, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, its meaning: its darkness receded. Zayd ibn Aslam said the same, and al-Farra' affirmed it and reported a consensus upon it. Al-Mubarrad and al-Khalil said: it is from the words with opposite meanings (adad); it is said 'as'asa when its darkness approached, and 'as'asa when its darkness receded. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Mubarrad said: Allah swore by the approach of the night and its receding together.

By this, the choice of this verb is for its conveying both states, each being fit for an oath, since both are among the manifestations of power, for darkness is followed by light, and light is followed by darkness. This is concision (ijaz).

Then the oath by the dawn is joined to it, at the time of its breathing, i.e., the splitting of its light, due to the correspondence with the mention of the night, and because the breathing of dawn is among the manifestations of the wondrous order that Allah placed in this world.

Al-tanaffus: its reality is the emergence of breath from a living being; it is used figuratively for the appearance of light along with remnants of darkness, by likening the emergence of light to the emergence of breath, in the manner of the explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah). Or, because when dawn appears a breeze comes with it, and this is made like breathing for it, in the manner of the implicit metaphor (makniyyah), by likening the dawn to one who has breath, along with likening the breeze to breaths.

The pronoun in "innahu" refers to the Qur'an, though no prior mention of it has occurred; but it is known from the context, in the setting of the report of the occurrence of the Resurrection, for it is among what the Qur'an informed them of, and they denied the Qur'an on account of that.

"Al-rasul al-karim" may be intended to refer to Jibril (peace be upon him). Jibril is described as a messenger because he is sent by Allah to the Prophet (ﷺ) with the Qur'an.

Page 155

The attribution of "qawl" (speech) to "rasul" is either due to the slightest connection, that Jibril conveys the words of the Qur'an to the Prophet (ﷺ) and relates them as Allah commanded him, so he is their speaker, i.e., its words proceed from him. In describing Jibril with the attribute "messenger" there is an indication that the speech he conveys is a message from Allah which he is commanded to deliver as it is.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: others said the messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ) throughout the whole verse. He did not name any of the exegetes who said this.

Within the praise of the Qur'an, praise of the angel sent with it is digressively included, to exalt the Qur'an. So the attributes of praise for a messenger are applied for exalting him too, and as an implicit indication that what was revealed through him is truthful, since the perfection of the speaker indicates the truth of the speech.

"Rasul" is described with five attributes. The first: karim, which is the precious in its kind.

The second and third attributes: "endowed with power, held in high esteem by the Lord of the Throne." Quwwah (power) in its reality is the capacity of an essence to perform great acts which are generally beyond reach. Among the attributes of Allah is "al-Qawiyy" (the Powerful), and among its forms is the capacity of a being, whether human or animal, to perform many acts which others of its kind cannot.

Its opposite is weakness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is the One who created you in weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair﴾ [al-Rum: 54].

Quwwah is also used figuratively for the steadfastness of the soul in its purpose, boldness, and firmness of heart. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12], and said: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. So describing Jibril as "endowed with power" may be intensity of capacity, as he was described in His words: ﴿possessor of strength﴾ [al-Najm: 6]; and it may be from the figurative strength, which is steadfastness in carrying out what he was sent with, as in His words: ﴿taught by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5], since what suits teaching is the strength of the soul. As for when the intended one is Muhammad (ﷺ), his description as "endowed with power with the Lord of the Throne" means the figurative sense, namely honor and acceptance of him.

Page 156

Al-makin is a fa'il form, an adjective from makan (makanah), with the damma on the kaf, meaning his rank became elevated in the sight of others. Allah the Exalted said in the story of Yusuf with the king: ﴿So when he spoke to him, he said: Indeed you are today with us established and trusted﴾ [Yusuf: 54].

Placing "ʿinda dhi al-ʿarsh" between "dhu quwwah" and "makin" so that both attributes govern it, in concision; i.e., he is possessed of power with Allah, meaning Allah made Jibril's capacity empower him to undertake the great tasks Allah entrusts to him, which require strength of power and strength of management; and he has rank with Allah and nearness.

The Prophet (ﷺ) is described with this in the same manner as previously mentioned.

"ʿInd" here is the nearness of honor and care, so "ʿinda" is for the figurative place, which carries the sense of special favor and nearness.

The reference was shifted from the Name of Majesty (Allah) to "dhi al-ʿarsh" with respect to Jibril, to represent the state of Jibril and his station with Allah by the condition of a prince who executes the king's command while being in a place of honor before him.

As for the Prophet (ﷺ), it is an indication of his great status, since he is endowed with power with the Lord of the greatest existent in status.

The fourth attribute: "obeyed," meaning that those angels with him obey him as an army obeys its commander; or, the Prophet (ﷺ) is obeyed, i.e., commanded that people obey what he commands them.

"Thamma" with a fatha on the tha' is a demonstrative of place, and what it refers to is the figurative place indicated by His words "ʿinda dhi al-ʿarsh." So the adverbial phrase may be connected to "muta'" (obeyed), which is more suitable for applying the attribute to Jibril, meaning: obeyed in the highest assembly in what he commands the angels; and the Prophet (ﷺ) is obeyed in the upper world, i.e., it is established with Allah that he be obeyed in what he commands.

It may also be connected to "amin" (trustworthy), and its placement before its complement is for emphasis on that place. The attribute applied to Jibril is evident, and the attribute applied to the Prophet (ﷺ) is because his trustworthiness is established in the highest assembly.

Page 157

"Al-amin" is one who guards what has been entrusted to him until he delivers it without deficiency or alteration. It is a fa'il form either in the sense of maf'ul (passive), i.e., one who is trusted, from amina-hu 'ala kadha; and according to this one says "imra'ah amin" (a trustworthy woman) and not "amina". Or it is an adjective of the form ashamm from amuna (with a damma on the mim), when trustworthiness has become his natural disposition; and according to this sense one says "imra'ah amina", and from it the statement of the jurists concerning a woman complaining of her husband's harm: they are to be placed with a trustworthy woman and a trustworthy man.
