As for the Prophet (ﷺ), it is an indication of his great status, since he is endowed with power with the Lord of the greatest existent in status.

The fourth attribute: "obeyed," meaning that those angels with him obey him as an army obeys its commander; or, the Prophet (ﷺ) is obeyed, i.e., commanded that people obey what he commands them.

"Thamma" with a fatha on the tha' is a demonstrative of place, and what it refers to is the figurative place indicated by His words "ʿinda dhi al-ʿarsh." So the adverbial phrase may be connected to "muta'" (obeyed), which is more suitable for applying the attribute to Jibril, meaning: obeyed in the highest assembly in what he commands the angels; and the Prophet (ﷺ) is obeyed in the upper world, i.e., it is established with Allah that he be obeyed in what he commands.

It may also be connected to "amin" (trustworthy), and its placement before its complement is for emphasis on that place. The attribute applied to Jibril is evident, and the attribute applied to the Prophet (ﷺ) is because his trustworthiness is established in the highest assembly.

Page 157

"Al-amin" is one who guards what has been entrusted to him until he delivers it without deficiency or alteration. It is a fa'il form either in the sense of maf'ul (passive), i.e., one who is trusted, from amina-hu 'ala kadha; and according to this one says "imra'ah amin" (a trustworthy woman) and not "amina". Or it is an adjective of the form ashamm from amuna (with a damma on the mim), when trustworthiness has become his natural disposition; and according to this sense one says "imra'ah amina", and from it the statement of the jurists concerning a woman complaining of her husband's harm: they are to be placed with a trustworthy woman and a trustworthy man.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 81, verse 22:**

﴿Your companion is not mad.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir: 19]. So it falls within the complement of the oath (khabar al-qasam) as a second answer to the oath. The meaning is: the Qur'an is not the word of a madman, as you claim. After Allah praised the Qur'an by saying it is the word of a messenger sent from Allah, and this included praise of the Prophet ﷺ as truthful in what he conveyed from Allah the Exalted, He followed it with refuting the slander of the polytheists against the Prophet ﷺ, namely their saying "a taught madman" and their saying ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾ [Saba': 8]. He refuted their claim with an emphatic and reinforced refutation. Its emphasis comes from the oath and from the added bāʾ after the negation. Its reinforcement comes from what the description "your companion" points to, namely that the one who conveyed it is your companion. The word "companion" (ṣāḥib) is a metonymy (kināya) for their knowing his character and his intellect, and knowing that he is not mad. It is the nature of a companion that the subtle details of his states are not hidden from his associates.

The meaning is: negating that the Qur'an comes from the whisperings of madmen. The soundness of its conveyor from madness requires the soundness of his speech from being mere whispering.

According to what was said earlier, that the intended referent of "a noble messenger" is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the phrase "your companion" here is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (iẓhār fī maqām al-iḍmār). It hints indirectly that he is known among them for soundness of mind and the solidity of his judgment.

The basic meaning of ṣāḥib (companion) is one who has ṣuḥba (companionship), which is constant association, whether in states of gathering or separation, for intimacy and agreement. From this comes the saying of a wife as ṣāḥiba, and of a traveller with someone else as ṣāḥib. Imru' al-Qays said:

*My companion wept when he saw the road before him*

Allah the Exalted said, quoting Yusuf: ﴿O two companions of the prison﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. Al-Hariri said in the twenty-first maqama: "And you have from me nothing but the companionship of the ship."

They also widely extend its use to one who mixes with another in many states, even in evil. Like the saying of al-Hajjaj addressing the Kharijites: "Were you not my companions in al-Ahwaz when you intended treachery and concealed disbelief?" And like the saying of al-Fadl al-Lahabi:

*Each has an intention to hate his companion, / by the grace of Allah we bear you and you bear us.*

The meaning is: the one you oppose, deny, and describe as mad is not mad, and you associate with him, accompany him, and know his reality. So your saying about him that he is mad is only for the purpose of slander and damaging his reputation.

This is the place of this sentence with what comes before and after it. The purpose of it is to establish the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ. It should not occur to the mind that it is set in the context of comparing and preferring between Jibril and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, and affirming the virtues of each of them, so that from the abundance of the attributes applied to Jibril one smells that he is superior to Muhammad ﷺ, or that the emphasis on the attributes of Jibril together with restraint in describing Muhammad ﷺ indicates the preference of the first over the second.

Among the most vulgar speech and weakest argumentation is the saying of the author of al-Kashshaf: "It is enough for you as evidence of the greatness of the rank of Jibril, peace be upon him, and the distinction of his station from the station of the best of humankind, Muhammad ﷺ, if you compare the two mentions and weigh his saying ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir: 19], ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne secure﴾ [al-Takwir: 20], ﴿obeyed there and trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir: 21], with his saying ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾." End.

How did his attention turn away from the context of the verse, which refutes the statements of the polytheists about the Prophet ﷺ, while they said nothing about Jibril? Because al-Zamakhshari aimed to draw from the verse evidence for the position of the Mu'tazilites on preferring angels over prophets. That is a question with another place for discussion. Moreover, you have learned that the attributes applied to a messenger in the saying of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir: 19] up to His saying "trustworthy" are not definitively limited to being applied to Jibril,

(Page 159)

since they are open to being applied to Muhammad ﷺ. The love of seeking evidence for the doctrines of the Mu'tazilites may overwhelm him with an overwhelming that throws his understanding into the pits of error. Would anyone with a grain of knowledge of the ways of wise speech permit himself to undertake explaining the excellence of one person by negating madness from him? All of this is based on interpreting ﴿a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir: 19] as Jibril. But if it is intended to mean Muhammad ﷺ, or both him and Jibril, peace be upon them both, then this argument is uprooted entirely.

It is not hidden that the shift from the proper name of the Prophet to "your companion" is for what "your companion" indicates of their knowledge of his states. As for the shift from the pronoun, if "messenger" is intended to refer specifically to the Prophet ﷺ, then it is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun for the reason mentioned. If both are intended by "messenger," then the mention of "your companion" is to restrict the speech to him.

Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on surah 81, verse 23:

﴿وَلَقَدْ رَآهُ بِالْأُفُقِ الْمُبِينِ﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿And your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwir: 22].

The connection between the two clauses is that when the polytheists learned that the Messenger (ﷺ) reported that Gabriel had come down to him with the revelation from the time of the cave of Hira onward, they mocked and said: "That which appears to him is a jinn." So God refuted them by negating madness from him, and then by affirming that he had seen Gabriel, the strong and trustworthy. The pronoun of subject refers to "companion" in His words ﴿your companion﴾, and the pronoun of object refers to "a noble Messenger". The context of nobility clarifies the referent of the seer and the seen.

Al-Ufuq (the horizon): the expanse that appears to the eye from the atmospheric sphere between the two extremes of the sunrise and sunset, from where the light of dawn shines and the twilight of sunset appears. It appears as if it were a blue dome. The meaning is: he saw him between the heaven and the earth.

Al-Mubin: an attribute of al-ufuq, that is, the clear, evident horizon.

The purpose of this description is to characterise the horizon from which Gabriel appeared to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon both of them, as a clear, evident horizon in which visible things are not confused and in which imagination does not deceive, and this attribute was made a sign that the one seen was an angel and not an illusion. This is because the illusions that madmen imagine are imagined by them on the earth, following what they were accustomed to from the time of their sanity. The Prophet, peace be upon him, described the angel he saw at the descent of the surah al-Muddaththir as sitting on a chair between the heaven and the earth. For this reason, the mention of the angel's appearance at the horizon is repeated in surah al-Najm, in His words: ﴿He was taught by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5] ﴿Endowed with strength, and he stood firm﴾ [al-Najm: 6] ﴿while he was at the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7] ﴿then he drew near and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8] ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 9], up to His saying: ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12] ﴿And he saw him another time﴾ [al-Najm: 13] ﴿at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 14] ﴿near which is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15], and the verses that follow. It has been said that the Prophet saw Gabriel, peace be upon both of them, in Mecca from the direction of the mountain of Ajyad, from its eastern side.

صفحة ١٦٠

The pronoun refers to "your companion" (ṣāḥibukum), as the context requires, since the polytheists did not claim that Jibril was niggardly with the unseen. They made that claim about the Prophet ﷺ, out of injustice and falsehood, and because the Return (al-ma'ād) was near.

Al-ghayb (the unseen) is what is absent from people's direct observation, or from their knowledge. It is a verbal noun used as a name (tasmiyah bi'l-maṣdar).

What is meant is what God has kept exclusively to His knowledge, except what He discloses to some of His prophets. This includes the revelation of the laws (wahy al-sharā'i'), knowledge of God's attributes and affairs, and the witnessing of the angel of revelation. This was discussed earlier, at His words: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word ﴿بِضَنِينٍ﴾ is written in the codices of the regional centres (maṣāḥif al-amṣār) with the unpointed ḍād (ḍād sāqiṭah), as the readers (al-qurrā', the Qur'an reciters) agreed.

It is related from Abu 'Ubayd, and al-Tabari said: "It is what the codices of the Muslims agree upon, even though their recitations differ concerning it."

In al-Kashshāf (by al-Zamakhshari) it is stated that in the codex of Ubayy it is written with ḍād, and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud with ẓā' (ẓā'). Al-Shāṭibī, in his versified work on orthography (al-Manẓūmah fī al-Rasm), abridged this, following the rasm of the codices with ḍād, when he said:

"The ḍād in *bi-ḍanīn* gathers the people (al-bashar)."

The readers differed in its recitation. Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir, 'Āṣim, Ḥamzah, Abu Ja'far, Khalaf, and Rawḥ from Ya'qub recited it with the unpointed ḍād (ḍād sāqiṭah), which emerges from the edge of the tongue on the side adjacent to the molars. This is the recitation that conforms to the rasm of the Imam codex.

[p. 161]

The rest recited it with the raised ẓā' (ẓā' mushallah), which emerges from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the upper front teeth. al-Kashshāf mentions that the Prophet ﷺ recited with both. This does not need pointing out, since the two recitations would not be mutawātir (transmitted by a multiplicity of reliable chains, so as to exclude any possibility of collusion in falsehood) unless each had been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ.

The ḍād and the ẓā' are two different letters, and words formed from one of them usually differ in meaning, except for examples such as *ḥuḍaḍ* with two unpointed ḍāds, *ḥuẓaẓ* with two raised ẓā's, and *ḥuḍaẓ* with an unpointed ḍād followed by a raised ẓā'. All three are with a ḍammah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on what follows the ḥā'. They have said that these are dialectal variants (lughāt) of a single word with one meaning, which is the name of a gum called *khawlān*.

There is no doubt that those who recited it with the raised ẓā' are among the readers of the mutawātir recitations, namely Ibn Kathīr, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisā'ī, and Ruways from Ya'qub. They transmitted it as mutawātir from the Prophet ﷺ. For this reason, the fact that their recitation differs from all the copies of the codices of the regional centres does not discredit it, because the mutawātir transmission of the recitation is stronger than the mutawātir transmission of the written text, if the written text is considered to have mutawātir transmission.

The condition mentioned, that a recitation must agree with what is in the codex of 'Uthmān in order to be a sound recitation that may be recited, applies only to the recitations that were not transmitted as mutawātir, as we explained in the sixth introduction (muqaddimah) of this commentary.

Abu 'Ubaydah offered an explanation for the agreement of the codices of the Imam on writing it with ḍād, despite the existence of a difference between ḍād and ẓā' in the mutawātir recitations. He said: "This is not a contradiction of the Book, because the ḍād and the ẓā' do not differ in their written form in the codices except by the addition of the head of one of them over the head of the other, so this may resemble and come close." End of quotation.

By this statement he means that what was written in the Imam codex is not a departure by the scribes of the codices from the mutawātir recitations. That is, they took into account the differences among the mutawātir recitations, so that they wrote some copies of the codices in consideration of the differences of recitation, which is the usual practice. Here, however, the orthography became ambiguous, and so the ẓā' came out with a small head.

I do not see any need for this excuse, because when the two recitations were mutawātir from the Prophet ﷺ, the scribes of the codices relied on one of them, which is the one recited by the majority of the Companions and especially 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān, and they left the other recitation to the memorization of the reciters.

[p. 162]

When the recitation *bi-ḍanīn* with the unpointed ḍād and *bi-ẓanīn* with the raised ẓā' are both mutawātir, we know that God revealed it in both ways, and that He intended both meanings.

As for the meaning of *ḍanīn* with the unpointed ḍād: it is *bakhīl*, one who does not give what he has. It is derived from *al-ḍann* (stinginess) with ḍād, the verbal noun of *ḍanna*, and when one is stingy, the present tense is with fatḥah or kasrah.

It may be on its literal meaning, that is: "Your companion is not stingy," meaning, he does not withhold what is revealed to him and what he tells of the unseen matters, in order to benefit from what he tells, such that he would not inform you of it except in exchange for a reward you give him. This is a metonymy (kināyah) for the negation that he is a soothsayer (kāhin) or a diviner ('arrāf) who receives news from the jinn. The polytheists used to frequent the soothsayers and claimed that they informed them of hidden matters. God said: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 41], ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 42]. Thus He established for them the distinction between the state of the soothsayers and the state of the Prophet ﷺ, by indicating that the Prophet does not ask them for any reward for what he tells them, whereas the soothsayer takes payment for what he tells, which they call *ḥulwān*. This meaning is of the same kind as His words: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾ [al-Furqān: 57], ﴿and I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 109], and the like.

It may also be that *ḍanīn* is a metaphorical (majāz) metonymy (majāz mursal) for concealment, by the relation of necessity ('alāqat al-luzūm), because concealment is a kind of stinginess with a matter that is known to the one who conceals it. That is: "He is not one who conceals the unseen," meaning what is revealed to him. They used to say: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ [Yūnus: 15], and they said: ﴿And we will not believe in your ascending until you bring down upon us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isrā': 93].

*'alā al-ghayb* (upon the unseen) is connected to *bi-ḍanīn* (with stingy).

In this interpretation the particle *'alā* carries the meaning of *bi* (with), like His words: ﴿Worthy of me not to say anything about God except the truth﴾ [al-A'rāf: 105], meaning "worthy by me" (ḥaqīq bī). Alternatively, *ḍanīn* is taken to imply the meaning of *ḥarīṣ* (greedy, eager), and greed is the extreme of stinginess. The meaning is: "Muhammad is not one who conceals anything of the unseen. Whatever he tells you is the very thing We revealed to him." In this case, the stingy one may be a metonymy for the concealer, which is a metonymy of another rank

[p. 163]

for non-alteration. The meaning is: "Your companion does not conceal any of the unseen," meaning, what he tells you is the truth.

As for the meaning of *ẓanīn* with the raised ẓā': it is *faʻīl* in the sense of *mafʻūl* (passive), derived from *al-ẓann* in the sense of accusation (tuhmah), that is, *maẓnūn* (suspected). It means that he is suspected of evil, that is, that he might be lying in what he tells of the unseen. The object of *ẓanīn* in this sense is frequently omitted in speech, until *al-ẓann* came to be used in the sense of accusation and was made transitive to a single object. The origin of this is that they say: *ẓanna bihi sū'an* (he suspected him of evil), so it transits to its first complement by the preposition *bi*. When this usage became common, they dropped the *bā'* and connected the verb directly to the genitive noun, so it became an object, and they said *ẓannahu* meaning *ittahamahu* (he accused him). It is said: "Such-and-such was stolen from me, and I suspect so-and-so."

The particle *'alā* in this interpretation is for figurative elevation (al-isti'lā' al-majāzī), which carries the meaning of location, like His words: ﴿Or I may find upon the fire a guidance﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 10], meaning "he is not accused concerning the matter of the unseen, which is the revelation, that he may not have conveyed it as it was." That is, what he conveyed is the unseen, about which there is no doubt. The opposite of this is their saying: *i'tamanahu 'alā kadhā* (he entrusted him with such-and-such).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 81, verse 25:

﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir: 19]. This is a return to what He swore to, that the Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger, after He digressed between them with those digressions which indicate the increase in the perfection of this speech through the sanctity of its source, the high station of its bearer with Allah, and the truthfulness of its recipient in receiving it from a true vision in which there is no imagination. Thus the transition back to purifying the Qur'an came by way of the mention of the unseen in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾ [al-Takwir: 24].

Indeed, the Qur'an is of the matter of the unseen that was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, and in it there are many reports about matters of the unseen, such as Paradise and Hellfire and the like.

It is known that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, because He informed about the pronoun with "speech," which is of the category of utterance, when He said: ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil.﴾ So the thing informed about is necessarily of the category of utterances. Therefore it should not be supposed that the pronoun refers to what the pronoun of ﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾ [al-Takwir: 24] refers to.

صفحة ١٦٤
This is a refutation of the claim of the polytheists about him: that he is a soothsayer (kahin). They used to claim that devils bring the soothsayers reports of the unseen. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42]. He also said: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able﴾. He also said: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 221] ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 222]. They used to claim that the soothsayer would receive from his devil, and they named his devil "ra'iy" (companion).

In the report about the interruption of revelation and the revelation of Surat al-Duha: that the carrier of firewood, the wife of Abu Lahab, who is Umm Jamil bint Harb, said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I see that your devil has forsaken you."

"Rajim" is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), i.e., "marjum" (stoned/cast out). The "marjum" is the one who is distanced, from whose evil people keep far; when he approaches them they stone him. So it is a descriptive attribute that reveals the devil, because he is not except one disowned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 81, verse 26:

﴿So where are you going?﴾

The clause ﴿So where are you going?﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD, interjected clause) between the clause ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾ [al-Takwir: 25] and His saying: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ [al-Takwir: 27].

The fa' (the "fa" particle) is for deriving (tafri') reproach and rebuke from the preceding proofs, which establish that the Qur'an cannot be the speech of a soothsayer (kahin), and that it is a revelation from God through the angel (malak).

This is an instance of a parenthetical clause being joined with the fa', as was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him remember it﴾ ['Abasa: 12] in Surah 'Abasa.

ayna (where) is an interrogative noun asking about place. It is a rhetorical interrogative (istifham inkari) about the place of their going, i.e., the path of their misguidance, representing the state of those who pursue the paths of falsehood by the state of one who has lost the straight road, so that someone asks him in disapproval of his conduct, meaning: turn away from this path, for it is a path of misguidance.

It is also permissible for the interrogation to be used to express incapacitation (ta'jiz), regarding the seeking of a path that they might travel to their goal of slandering the Qur'an.

The meaning is: the paths of your calumny have been closed off to you, since the falsity of your claim that the Qur'an is the speech of a madman or the speech of a soothsayer has become clear through the decisive proof. So what will you claim after that?

Know that the clause ﴿where are you going﴾ has been used as a proverb (mathal), and perhaps it is one of the novel expressions of the Qur'an. I have seen in the speech of some people: "Where is he taking you?", said to one who is in error and blindness.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 81, verses 27–28:**

﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ ﴿for whoever among you wills to take the straight path﴾.

After He had restored them from their misguidance, He directed them to the reality of the Qur'an by His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds.﴾ This sentence functions as an emphasis (ta'kid) of the sentence ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾ [al-Takwir: 25]. For this reason it is detached from a conjunction. The restriction (qasr, exclusive limitation) derived from the negation and exception in His saying ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ indicates that the Qur'an is restricted to the attribute of being a reminder, meaning: nothing other than that. This is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), intended to negate that it is the word of a poet, or the word of a soothsayer, or the word of a madman. Among what the restriction conveys is the negation that it is the word of an accursed devil, and thus the verse contains an emphasis of ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾ [al-Takwir: 25].

The word "dhikr" (reminder) is a term that comprises the meanings of supplication, admonition toward good deeds, and warning against falsehood and misguidance. That is: the Qur'an is nothing but a reminder for all people, by which they benefit in the soundness of their belief, their obedience to their Lord, the refinement of their morals, the manners some of them observe with others, the preservation of their rights, the enduring order of their community, and how they deal with other nations that did not follow it.

"Al-'alamin" (the worlds) encompasses all of mankind, because they are all called to be guided by it and to benefit from what it contains.

If you say: The Qur'an includes the narratives of the prophets and nations, and it is also a miracle (mu'jizah) for Muhammad (ﷺ). How then is it restricted to being a reminder?

I say: A relative restriction is only intended to specify an attribute to its bearer in relation to another particular attribute. Moreover, you may make the restriction an absolute one (qasr haqiqi), indicating that the Qur'an is restricted to being a reminder and not other attributes. The narratives and reports it contains are intended for admonition and lesson, as I have explained in the Seventh Introduction.

[Page 166]

As for its miraculousness (i'jaz), it has a great role in reminding, because its inimitability is proof that it is not a speech produced by human beings. When this is known, certainty arises that it is true.

The phrase ﴿for whoever among you wills to take the straight path﴾ is substituted for "to the worlds" as a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull, substitution of part for whole). The preposition governing the substituted element is repeated with the substitute to emphasize the governing element, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters hanging low﴾ [al-An'am: 99], and His saying: ﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]. This was discussed in Surat al-An'am. The address in His saying "among you" is to those who were addressed by His saying: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾ [al-Takwir: 26]. Since the Qur'an is a reminder to them, and they are among the "worlds," the mention of ﴿for whoever among you wills to take the straight path﴾ applies to the rest of the worlds as well, by the rule of qiyas al-musawat (analogy of equality). Thus the speech contains an implicit indication (kinaya) to that effect.

The purpose of this substitution is to draw attention to the fact that those who were reminded by the Qur'an, namely the Muslims, have willed uprightness for themselves, and so they advised their own souls. This is a commendation of them.

In the implication of the relative clause (mafhum al-silah) there is an allusion that those who were not reminded by the Qur'an were prevented from being reminded only because they did not will to be upright. Rather, they were content for themselves with crookedness, that is, corruption of deed and belief, so that the listeners may know that the persistence of those people in error is not due to the Qur'an's inadequacy in guiding them, but because they refused to be guided by it, either out of obstinacy, as they used to say: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat: 5], or out of turning away from receiving it: ﴿And those who disbelieved said: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may prevail﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

"Istiqamah" (uprightness) is used metaphorically for the soundness of inner action, which is belief, and outer action, which is deeds and words, likening action to a straight line, a comparison of the intelligible to the perceptible. Furthermore, those who did not will to be upright are the disbelievers in the Qur'an, and they are the primary addressees of the speech. Those among the Muslims who fell short in being guided by some part of the Qur'an are also included, to varying degrees, for he did not will uprightness in what he neglected, in certain states, times, or places.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 81, verses 27–28:**

﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ ﴿for whoever among you wills to take the straight path﴾.

After He had restored them from their misguidance, He directed them to the reality of the Qur'an by His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds.﴾ This sentence functions as an emphasis (ta'kid) of the sentence ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾ [al-Takwir: 25]. For this reason it is detached from a conjunction. The restriction (qasr, exclusive limitation) derived from the negation and exception in His saying ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ indicates that the Qur'an is restricted to the attribute of being a reminder, meaning: nothing other than that. This is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), intended to negate that it is the word of a poet, or the word of a soothsayer, or the word of a madman. Among what the restriction conveys is the negation that it is the word of an accursed devil, and thus the verse contains an emphasis of ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾ [al-Takwir: 25].

The word "dhikr" (reminder) is a term that comprises the meanings of supplication, admonition toward good deeds, and warning against falsehood and misguidance. That is: the Qur'an is nothing but a reminder for all people, by which they benefit in the soundness of their belief, their obedience to their Lord, the refinement of their morals, the manners some of them observe with others, the preservation of their rights, the enduring order of their community, and how they deal with other nations that did not follow it.

"Al-'alamin" (the worlds) encompasses all of mankind, because they are all called to be guided by it and to benefit from what it contains.

If you say: The Qur'an includes the narratives of the prophets and nations, and it is also a miracle (mu'jizah) for Muhammad (ﷺ). How then is it restricted to being a reminder?

I say: A relative restriction is only intended to specify an attribute to its bearer in relation to another particular attribute. Moreover, you may make the restriction an absolute one (qasr haqiqi), indicating that the Qur'an is restricted to being a reminder and not other attributes. The narratives and reports it contains are intended for admonition and lesson, as I have explained in the Seventh Introduction.

[Page 166]

As for its miraculousness (i'jaz), it has a great role in reminding, because its inimitability is proof that it is not a speech produced by human beings. When this is known, certainty arises that it is true.

The phrase ﴿for whoever among you wills to take the straight path﴾ is substituted for "to the worlds" as a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull, substitution of part for whole). The preposition governing the substituted element is repeated with the substitute to emphasize the governing element, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters hanging low﴾ [al-An'am: 99], and His saying: ﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]. This was discussed in Surat al-An'am. The address in His saying "among you" is to those who were addressed by His saying: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾ [al-Takwir: 26]. Since the Qur'an is a reminder to them, and they are among the "worlds," the mention of ﴿for whoever among you wills to take the straight path﴾ applies to the rest of the worlds as well, by the rule of qiyas al-musawat (analogy of equality). Thus the speech contains an implicit indication (kinaya) to that effect.

The clause may be a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*, a closing sentence that restates or reinforces the point) or a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*, a clause placed between parts of a sentence) at the end of the speech.

It may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the purpose is completion (*takmil*) and a precautionary qualification (*ihtiras*) in the sense of "for whoever among you wills to go straight," meaning: "and for whoever among the worlds wills that for himself." Earlier, at the end of Surat al-Insan, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19] ﴿So whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19] ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan: 30].

The difference between this verse and that one is that in this verse Allah is described as ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, and this description implies the reason (*ta'lil*) for linking the will of whoever among the worlds wills to go straight to the will of Allah. That is because He is Lord of the worlds: He is the Creator within them of the motives of will and of the chain of causes (*asbab*) by which it comes about, and He is the One who guided them to remain upright upon the truth. Through this description the closer connection becomes evident between the people's will to go straight by means of the Qur'an and the Qur'an being a reminder to the worlds.

As for the verse of Surat al-Insan, it is concluded with ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan: 30], meaning: He, in His knowledge and wisdom, attaches His will for them to go straight to the places where they are fit for it. This indicates that whoever does not will to take to his Lord a way, Allah has deprived him, by His knowledge and wisdom, of His will for good; this is a metaphor (*kinaya*) for their wretchedness.

The particle *ma* is a negation, and the exception (*istithna'*) is from deleted verbal nouns (*masadir mahdhufa*) indicated by His saying ﴿except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30]. The explanation of this was given earlier in Surat al-Insan.

In this verse and the verse of Surat al-Insan there is a manifestation of the nobility of the people of uprightness, in that they are in the place of special care from their Lord when He wills uprightness for them and prepares them for it. This care has a great meaning, about which the people of knowledge were perplexed in trying to uncover it. Among them are those whose thinking swayed them toward determinism (*jabr*, the view that human beings have no real choice), and among them are those who plunged into the pit of predestination (*qadar*). Among them are those who held a balanced position and affirmed with firmness that the servants have a created power (*quwwa haditha*) by which they choose to follow good or evil. Some of these called it a created capability (*qudra haditha*) and some called it acquisition (*kasb*). They interpreted whatever in the apparent meanings of the verses and reports contradicted this as being in the context of Allah teaching His servants good manners in respect of His majesty.

This is the furthest that sound understandings have reached in reconciling the apparently conflicting verses of the Qur'an and the Prophetic traditions, and behind it there is a fine thread that binds it together, which understandings may fall short of grasping.

Surat al-Infitar

This surah is named (Surat al-Infitar) in the mushafs and in most of the tafsir works.

In a hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would like to look at the Day of Resurrection as if he were seeing it with his own eyes, let him recite ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1], and ﴿When the sky breaks apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1], and ﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1]." Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan gharib hadith." I have already explained the uncertainty in it at the beginning of Surat al-Takwir.

In some tafsir works it is called (Surat ﴿When the sky breaks apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1]), and by this name al-Bukhari titled it in the Book of Tafsir of his Sahih. The author of al-Itqan did not count it among the surahs with more than one name, and its name is al-Infitar.

The reason for the name is that the phrase (﴿When the sky breaks apart﴾ [al-Infitar: 1]) occurs at its beginning, so it became known by it.

It is called in a few tafsir works (Surat Infatarat), and it was said that it is called (Surat al-Munfatira), meaning: the sky that breaks apart.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is numbered the eighty-second in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Nazi'at and before Surat al-Inshiqaq.

The number of its verses is nineteen.

* * *

This surah includes: the affirmation of resurrection and the mention of the terrors that precede it;

[p. 170]
the awakening of the polytheists to consider the matters that have turned them away from acknowledging the Oneness of Allah the Exalted and from reflecting on the evidences for the occurrence of resurrection and recompense;

the information that deeds are recorded, and the explanation of the recompense for deeds, good and bad;

and the warning to people that they should not suppose that anything will save them from the requital of Allah for their evil deeds.
